ai.definition: Next-generation TB vaccines are a class of candidate vaccines designed to improve upon the limitations of the century-old BCG vaccine, with a focus on providing better protection against tuberculosis (TB), particularly for adults.
ai.howItWorks: These vaccines typically work by introducing specific components of Mycobacterium tuberculosis or using viral vectors to deliver genetic material from TB into the human body. This triggers an immune response that is expected to provide long-lasting protection against TB infection and disease.
ai.problemSolved: The current BCG vaccine has limited efficacy, especially in adults, and does not protect against all strains of TB. Next-generation vaccines aim to address these shortcomings by enhancing immunogenicity and broadening the range of protected strains.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacture involves complex biotechnological processes including cell culture, genetic engineering, and purification steps. The use of viral vectors requires specialized facilities due to biosafety concerns.
ai.buildProcess: The process begins with selecting or designing antigens or genetic material from M. tuberculosis, followed by vector development if using a viral vector. This is then scaled up through cell cultures and purified before being tested for safety and efficacy in preclinical studies.
ai.costDrivers: High R&D costs due to extensive testing, specialized equipment for viral vectors, and the need for large-scale clinical trials. Manufacturing costs are also high due to complex bioprocesses and regulatory requirements.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is cautiously optimistic as promising results from late-stage trials could lead to approval in the coming years, but commercialization faces challenges such as distribution logistics in low-resource settings.
ai.regulation: Subject to rigorous regulatory scrutiny by health authorities worldwide. Requires approval through phases of clinical trials and post-marketing surveillance.
ai.risks: Technical risks related to vaccine efficacy and safety, logistical challenges in global distribution, and potential market resistance due to established BCG use.
ai.profitability: Potential for high profitability if successful, but uncertain given the complex development process and regulatory hurdles. Market size is significant due to TB's global impact.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may include combination therapies with other drugs or vaccines, as well as improvements in delivery methods such as nasal sprays or oral formulations.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and refrigeration requirements during transport and storage.

glossary.def: A live-attenuated vaccine against tuberculosis that has been in use for over a century, but with limited efficacy in adults.
The bacterium responsible for causing tuberculosis. The target pathogen of TB vaccines.
A modified virus used to deliver genetic material into cells, often employed in next-generation vaccine development.

subsystems.name: Antigen design
subsystems.role: chooses the bacterial proteins the immune system should remember.

subsystems.name: Adjuvant or delivery system
subsystems.role: wakes up the immune system so the antigen provokes a strong, lasting response.

subsystems.name: Manufacturing
subsystems.role: makes the vaccine reproducibly at large scale.

subsystems.name: Stability and cold chain
subsystems.role: keeps the vaccine potent from factory to clinic.

subsystems.name: Immunology and readouts
subsystems.role: measures whether a candidate actually protects, since TB correlates of protection are poorly defined.

subsystems.name: Trial and delivery network
subsystems.role: runs late-stage efficacy trials and would introduce the vaccine where TB is common.

buildSteps.title: Pick the antigens
buildSteps.detail: Researchers select proteins that the bacterium expresses during infection and that the human immune system recognises, aiming for a target that BCG does not train the body to attack.

buildSteps.title: Build the candidate
buildSteps.detail: Antigens are produced as recombinant proteins, or packaged into a vector or an engineered live BCG-like strain.

buildSteps.title: Add the adjuvant
buildSteps.detail: The antigen is combined with an immune-stimulating formulation, because proteins alone provoke weak, short-lived responses.

buildSteps.title: Test in animals
buildSteps.detail: Mice, guinea pigs and non-human primates are challenged with TB to see whether the candidate reduces bacterial burden or disease.

buildSteps.title: Run early human trials
buildSteps.detail: Phase 1 and 2 studies check safety, dose and immune response, usually first in adults with and without prior BCG.

buildSteps.title: Prove efficacy in the field
buildSteps.detail: Large phase 2b and phase 3 trials in high-burden countries follow tens of thousands of participants for years, since only a small fraction develop active TB.

buildSteps.title: License and prequalify
buildSteps.detail: Regulators review the data; WHO prequalification opens the door to procurement by low- and middle-income countries.

buildSteps.title: Deploy
buildSteps.detail: A licensed vaccine would be added to infant or adolescent schedules, or given to adults with latent infection to stop reactivation.

prerequisites.tech: Adjuvant systems that drive cellular immunity
prerequisites.why: TB needs a T-cell response, not just antibodies; modern adjuvant platforms can do this.

prerequisites.tech: Live attenuated and vector vaccine platforms
prerequisites.why: recombinant BCG and viral-vectored candidates build on established vaccine engineering.

prerequisites.tech: Large trial infrastructure in high-burden settings
prerequisites.why: efficacy trials need tens of thousands of participants and years of follow-up in places with working TB diagnosis.
without an immune marker that predicts protection, every candidate must be tested in a full efficacy trial.
a successful vaccine would need hundreds of millions of doses made affordably.

pathway.milestone: Late-stage candidates in phase 3, including a protein-plus-adjuvant vaccine and a recombinant BCG; BCG revaccination tested in adolescents
pathway.unlocks: the first real evidence in decades on whether a new TB vaccine can work at scale.
regulatory review and WHO policy recommendations, if protection holds.
procurement by national immunisation programmes in high-burden countries.

pathway.milestone: Introduction into routine schedules, combined with better diagnostics and shorter treatment
pathway.unlocks: a credible path to bending the global TB epidemic.
